strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: improving precision of autoregressive VLAs at test time without requiring an external trained verifier.
Proposes a novel internal confidence metric based on KL divergence from condition-masking distributions, together with a joint training strategy that exposes the model to masked conditions.
Evaluates on multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and real-world Franka experiments, covering two base VLA architectures (π0-FAST and OpenVLA).
Reports notable real-world gains (e.g., 28% relative in-distribution and 35% out-of-distribution improvement) and strong low-data improvements on RoboCasa.
Includes useful ablations on sampling strategy, candidate number, masking variants, joint training, aggregation, and a single-prefetch deployment optimization.
Provides reproducibility details such as training hyperparameters, compute resources, and deployment configuration.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea adapts self-certainty / KL-based confidence to VLA Best-of-N sampling, and the ablation shows only a small gain over simple likelihood-based selection.

Theoretical grounding is limited: there is no formal guarantee that the condition-masked distribution represents maximum uncertainty or that higher KL divergence selects more correct action sequences; key choices such as regularization temperature and first-5-token aggregation are largely heuristic.

The abstract/claims state that the method requires no additional training, but the main results rely on joint training with condition dropout, which is additional target-task training and contradicts the stated advantage.

Evaluation has statistical limitations: real-world results are based on small numbers of trials (24 per in-distribution task, 16 per out-of-distribution task) with no confidence intervals or significance tests, making the large relative gains less reliable.

Simulation gains are sometimes modest or inconsistent: LIBERO improvements are small on average and regress on some suites for OpenVLA and π0-FAST, and SIMPLER-WidowX average improvement is only about 3.4 percentage points.

Baselines are insufficient or not fully comparable: real-world experiments only compare against the base policy, with no trained-verifier or compute-matched test-time-scaling baselines, while several simulation baselines are taken from prior papers under different protocols.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and ad hoc tuning weaken generality: the best masking variant depends on the benchmark, N=4 is best but scaling is non-monotonic, and the aggregation strategy is tailored to the tokenizer/model.
The practical efficiency analysis is incomplete: Best-of-N still adds latency, and the paper does not provide a compute-accuracy trade-off against compute-matched baselines.

The scope is narrow, focusing mainly on pick-and-place tasks; there is little failure analysis, robustness testing beyond a small OOD set, or evidence that the method extends to broader manipulation domains.
No code release is mentioned, and the real-world dataset is not publicly available, limiting reproducibility of the most compelling results.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving precision of vision-language-action models via test-time scaling without an external verifier.
The proposed MG-Select is simple and, in its base form, does not require an external value model; it uses condition-masking KL divergence as an intrinsic confidence signal.
The paper evaluates on multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and real-world Franka tasks, and tests two autoregressive VLA backbones (pi0-FAST and OpenVLA).
Ablations examine several design choices, including sampling temperature, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, aggregation strategy, and inference latency.
The real-world out-of-distribution results show promising gains on unseen objects, suggesting the method may improve robustness in some settings.
The joint training strategy appears to provide a useful regularization effect and is a reasonable direction for making condition-masking distributions more reliable.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially a Best-of-N selection rule using KL divergence from a masked-condition reference, closely related to self-certainty/self-consistency for LLMs and classifier-free guidance. The paper does not adequately differentiate its technical contribution from these known ideas.

The central confidence metric is weakly justified. It is not clear why high KL(Q||P) from a condition-masking distribution should identify the most accurate action, especially when P is overconfident or wrong. The asymmetry of KL and the choice of Q are ad hoc and not theoretically or empirically calibrated.

The claim of being 'without additional training' is misleading. The strongest results use MG-Select* with joint training, which is additional fine-tuning. For SIMPLER-WidowX and real-world in-distribution tasks, only the joint-training variant is reported, so the gains cannot be attributed cleanly to test-time scaling.

Missing key baselines: despite motivating the work by the drawbacks of external verifiers, the paper never compares against value-guided or VLM-verifier test-time scaling methods (e.g., Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.). Without such comparisons, the claim that verifier-free selection is competitive is unsupported.

Hyperparameters are searched per benchmark and best results are reported (sampling temperature, N, masking variant, regularization temperature). There is no held-out validation split or sensitivity analysis, which compromises the fairness of the main comparisons.

Joint training alone produces large gains (e.g., RoboCasa pick-and-place 17.0 to 28.5), so a substantial part of the improvement may come from regularization/robustness rather than the proposed test-time selection mechanism. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle these effects.

Reported improvements are often modest: LIBERO average for pi0-FAST is 92.0 to 93.1, SIMPLER average is 46.9 to 50.3, and RoboCasa 300-demo all-task is 61.2 to 61.3/62.9. Some suites regress (OpenVLA LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal).
Real-world evaluation uses small trial counts (16 or 24 trials per task) with no confidence intervals or significance tests, making the 28%/35% claims fragile.

Ablation results suggest brittle design choices: best aggregation uses only the first 5 tokens, naive summation is worst, and the condition-masking distribution must be heavily temperature-smoothed (tau=4.0). These choices are dataset-specific and not principled.
The masking variants are selected per environment (state-masking for SIMPLER, text-masking for RoboCasa), which makes the method look tuned to each benchmark rather than generally applicable.
Scope is narrow: the method applies to autoregressive VLA tokenization and is not obviously applicable to diffusion/flow-based VLAs, which are also prominent.
The paper lacks failure analysis, limitations discussion, and safety/ethical consideration for real-world robot deployment.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, real-world details are sparse, and the extensive per-benchmark hyperparameter search makes exact reproduction difficult.
Latency overhead is not fully solved: single-prefill still increases latency with N (e.g., 30.4s vs 20.2s at N=16), and there is no latency comparison against external-verifier methods.

Reporting is inconsistent: the abstract attributes 28%/35% real-world gains to MG-Select, but Table 4 uses MG-Select* with joint training for in-distribution tasks while Table 3 uses MG-Select without joint training for out-of-distribution tasks.

strengths: Introduces a practical verifier-free test-time scaling method for autoregressive VLAs, using condition-masking distributional confidence to select among sampled action candidates without external verifiers or additional reward models.

The proposed joint training strategy with condition dropout is simple and effective: it improves the quality of the reference distribution and yields consistent gains, especially in low-data regimes (e.g., 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place with 30 demonstrations).

The empirical evaluation is broad: simulated benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) with multiple VLA backbones (π0-FAST, OpenVLA), varying demonstration counts, and real-world Franka experiments including in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks.

Ablation studies are thorough and informative, covering inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, sampling/regularization temperatures, confidence aggregation, and inference latency.
The single-prefill deployment optimization meaningfully reduces the latency overhead of Best-of-N sampling, making the method more practical for real-time robot control.
The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation, method description, and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines existing ideas—test-time scaling/Best-of-N selection, KL-based confidence/self-certainty, and condition dropout—adapted to autoregressive VLAs. There is no major conceptual or theoretical advance.

The paper lacks direct comparison to external-verifier test-time scaling methods (e.g., value-guided policies or RoboMonkey) on the same benchmarks. Since the central motivation is to avoid external verifiers, it is important to show competitiveness against those methods, not only against base VLAs and simple selection baselines.

Theoretical grounding for the confidence metric is weak. It is assumed that high KL divergence from a condition-masking distribution indicates a more confident and correct action, but a confidently wrong action can also have high KL. The claim that the reference distribution represents maximum uncertainty while remaining task-aligned is not formally justified or empirically validated.

Several key hyperparameters appear tuned per benchmark: masking variant, sampling temperature, regularization temperature, and aggregation strategy (e.g., summing first 5 tokens for π0-FAST vs. averaging for OpenVLA). This raises concerns about overfitting to the evaluation setups and limits the generality of the recommended recipe.

Some performance gains are modest and task-dependent. For example, on LIBERO with OpenVLA, MG-Select improves the average but decreases spatial performance; on SIMPLER, the eggplant task remains poor. Real-world results use relatively small numbers of trials, and variance/significance is not reported.

The best results require joint training with condition dropout, which is still an additional training procedure. The test-time scaling alone gives smaller gains, so the framing as fully training-free is somewhat overstated.

Potential safety and ethical implications of deploying a confidence-based selection method on real robots are not discussed. Selecting overconfident wrong actions could be risky in physical environments.

strengths: Proposes a verifier-free test-time scaling framework for autoregressive VLAs by using condition-masking distributional confidence, avoiding external verifier training and adding no extra model modules at inference.

Evaluated across several simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world Franka tasks, with ablations on masking variants, number of candidates, aggregation, joint training, and latency.
The joint condition-dropout training strategy is simple and appears to regularize the base VLA, and the single-prefill deployment substantially reduces latency for larger candidate sets.
Shows competitive performance against an external-verifier baseline (RoboMonkey) in an appendix comparison while using lower inference latency, and demonstrates strong low-data gains on RoboCasa.
Qualitative and token-level KL visualizations provide useful insight into when the confidence signal helps during alignment, grasping, and placement phases.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters such as masking variant, sampling temperature, number of candidates, aggregation strategy, and regularization temperature are selected by searching on each dataset and reporting the best result; this likely uses test-set tuning and can inflate reported gains. A held-out validation protocol is not clearly described, and final per-benchmark hyperparameters are not fully reported.

The main comparisons often report MG-Select* (joint training plus test-time scaling) against a base model without joint training. Joint training alone already gives substantial gains on RoboCasa (e.g., pick-and-place 17.0 to 28.5), so the incremental benefit of test-time scaling is not cleanly isolated on LIBERO, SIMPLER-WidowX, and real-world in-distribution tasks.

Absolute improvements are modest on several benchmarks, e.g., LIBERO average 92.0 to 93.1, with some task suites degrading. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported despite averaging over 3 seeds, so several gains could be within noise.

Verifier-based test-time scaling methods are not compared in the main experiments; the only comparison to RoboMonkey appears in an appendix and only for SIMPLER-WidowX. Since external-verifier approaches are the primary alternative, the verifier-free advantage is not fully established.

The condition-masking distributional confidence is heuristic and task-dependent; the method requires choosing which condition to mask for each environment, and the high-temperature regularization is ad hoc. Theoretical grounding for the confidence metric is limited.

Real-world evaluation covers only a small number of tasks and trials, and the chosen masking variants and hyperparameters for the real-world experiments are not specified. The claim of improved precision is supported mainly by task success rates rather than direct precision measurements.
Reproducibility is limited: no code, model checkpoints, or exact final hyperparameter configurations are provided, and the paper relies on appendix implementation details without a released artifact.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving VLA precision without external verifiers is practically useful, and test-time scaling for robot policies is timely.
Empirical evaluation is broad, covering RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-robot experiments, with multiple VLA backbones (pi0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA).

The proposed condition-masking distribution and joint training strategy are simple and can be implemented without external models; the single-prefill deployment reduces latency compared with naive parallel sampling.
Ablations study several design choices (number of candidates, masking variants, temperature, aggregation, dropout ratio) and provide some insight into behavior.
The paper is generally clear in presenting the high-level framework and includes implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core idea is Best-of-N selection using an internal KL-divergence confidence score against a condition-masked reference distribution, which is an incremental adaptation of existing self-certainty/verifier-free LLM test-time scaling to VLAs rather than a fundamentally new method.

The theoretical justification is weak: KL(Q||P) is not inherently a correctness or action-quality metric, and the paper does not justify why selecting the candidate with highest KL from the masked distribution should yield the most precise action. The entropy-temperature theorem is trivial and does not support the selection criterion.

The claim of being 'without additional training' is overstated: the strongest results require joint training with condition dropout (MG-Select*), which is a modified training procedure. Per-benchmark choices of masking variant, sampling temperature, regularization temperature, and aggregation token span also amount to significant task-specific tuning.

Evaluation lacks important test-time-scaling baselines: the paper does not compare with value-function-guided TTS or VLM-verifier methods on RoboCasa, LIBERO, or real-world tasks; the only comparison with RoboMonkey is on SIMPLER and is not consistently superior. Simple selection baselines such as entropy, max-probability, and other self-certainty variants are missing.

Some empirical gains are modest and unstable: on LIBERO, the average improvement is only +1.1 (92.0 to 93.1), with drops on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal; after joint training alone, the additional benefit of MG-Select is small (e.g., RoboCasa PnP 28.5 to 31.0).

Real-world results rely on small numbers of trials (e.g., 6 trials per task, 16 OOD trials) without confidence intervals or statistical tests, making the reported 28%/35% relative gains difficult to trust.
The method requires task-specific heuristics and hyperparameter search, which risks overfitting to the evaluated benchmarks and undermines the claim of general seamless applicability.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or model checkpoints are mentioned, the real-robot protocol is not fully specified, and the paper does not discuss failure cases or negative results beyond brief qualitative examples.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving precision of vision-language-action models without the overhead and generalization issues of external verifiers.
Proposes a simple and practical test-time scaling framework (MG-Select) that uses internal model signals rather than external modules.
Introduces condition-masking distributions as reference distributions and a joint training strategy with condition dropout to improve the reference quality.

Extensive evaluation across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world Franka experiments, covering multiple VLA architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA).
Thorough ablation studies on inference strategy, candidate number, masking variants, joint training, temperature, aggregation, dropout ratio, and latency.
Efficient deployment strategy with single prefill substantially reduces inference latency compared to vanilla MG-Select.
Competitive comparison with an external-verifier baseline (RoboMonkey) on SIMPLER-WidowX, with lower latency.
Clear writing and detailed implementation/reproducibility appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method combines existing ideas such as Best-of-N sampling, KL-based self-certainty/confidence from LLM literature, and condition dropout, resulting in an incremental contribution.

The proposed condition-masking reference distribution provides only marginal gains over simpler alternatives: on RoboCasa, uniform-KL and likelihood baselines are close to MG-Select (e.g., PnP 30.0/30.5 vs 31.0; All 46.5/46.8 vs 48.1), weakening the central claim that condition-masking is essential.

Many main results report MG-Select* with joint training, but joint-training-only baselines are missing on SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world experiments, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of test-time scaling from regularization/data augmentation. The RoboCasa ablation shows joint training alone accounts for a large portion of the gain.

Hyperparameter selection appears to be performed on the evaluation benchmarks: the paper states they search for optimal configurations on each dataset and report the best result, which risks test-set tuning and optimistic performance estimates.

No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported; several gains are small (e.g., LIBERO average 92.0→93.1 with drops on Spatial and Goal), and real-world trials are limited to 16–24 per task.
Claims such as 'without requiring additional training' are misleading because the best results rely on joint training; the framework is not purely test-time.

The external verifier generalization claim is not directly tested against the proposed method on out-of-distribution tasks; the comparison with RoboMonkey is limited to SIMPLER-WidowX and uses a modified verifier setup.
The aggregation strategy requires domain-specific tuning (first 1 token on SIMPLER-WidowX, first 5 on RoboCasa), suggesting a lack of general principle and potential fragility.
Real-world evaluation lacks comparison to other test-time scaling methods and a joint-training-only baseline.
No code release is mentioned, which may limit reproducibility despite detailed appendix.
